6.0.0.en: Under Elisha's care and visiting of the sons of the prophets their number increased and the place where they dwelt could no longer hold them, so they thought of dwelling beside the Jordan River, where there was a spacious place, and building houses for themselves there, and it would become easy for Elisha to visit them and teach them. They asked Elisha's leave for this and he agreed. Because they were poor, they built the houses themselves and made simple houses of timber. But the most important thing is that they asked Elisha to come with them, for the most important thing was that they keep his fatherhood, care, blessing and life-giving teachings, and this confirms their care for spiritual discipleship, as it confirms Elisha's fatherhood to them.

6.0.1.en: Take care to learn from your spiritual father and receive his blessing and carry out his guidance, and God will rejoice in your obedience and bless you, and you will grow in quietness and strength.

6.1.0.en: Elisha went with them, and as soon as they reached the Jordan they began to cut down timber and gather it. Perhaps he shared the work with them, or at least directed and supervised the work, and this shows his fatherhood and his love in sharing his children's work.

6.2.1.en: While one of them was felling timber, the iron axe head fell into the water, and he cried out at once, calling on Elisha for help and saying that the axe that had fallen was borrowed, for he did not own it and could not pay its price to its owner, since the sons of the prophets were poor and iron was a costly metal at that time. But out of this man's love for the work and sharing in his brothers' labor, he had borrowed this axe from a friend of his, and his position became embarrassing after it fell to the bottom of the river and it was very hard to recover it. But his sense of Elisha's fatherhood made him call on him, confident that he would not leave him.

6.3.0.en: Elisha asked him where it fell, and the man showed him the place, and Elisha cut down a stick and cast it in at the same place, and the iron swam on the surface of the water. Then Elisha said to him to take it up, and he put out his hand and took it.

6.3.1.en: The stick of wood is a type of the Cross of Christ, which restored to man the pure nature that he had lost through sin. We note here that Elisha uses a material in working the miracle, namely the stick of wood, as he used before the meal and the salt; he uses tangible and visible materials to suit man's bodily senses and to assure him of the completion of the miracle. Although the miracle seems small, since this axe could be done without, Elisha cared to work the miracle for the following reasons:

6.3.2.en: 1- To show his fatherhood and care for his children, for he feels their feelings and how this man was in embarrassment before his friend, from whom he had borrowed the axe.

6.3.3.en: 2- To declare to the sons of the prophets their human helplessness, and that they might feel the power of God that supports them, not only in building houses for themselves but in all their life, and so rely on Him.

6.3.4.en: Elisha did not lift the iron with his own hand, but made the man put out his hand and take the floating piece of iron, to strengthen his faith in the completion of the miracle, and on the other hand to have him share in it; man ought to do his duty, even if it is small, and the difficult thing God will do for him.

6.4.0.en: The state of Aram was a strong state, which is present-day Syria, but David the prophet subdued it to Israel, and it remained subject in the days of Solomon (1 Kgs 10:29). But afterward it began to rebel and fight the kingdom of Israel. The king of Aram at that time was called Benhadad, while the king of Israel was Joram. The king of Aram made secret plans with his servants for a surprise attack on Israel. He would set an ambush and fix a place to encamp, which no one knew except his private servants.

6.5.0.en: Elisha used to inform the king of Israel of the place where the king of Aram would be with his army, and warn him not to approach that place, because he would have to face the Aramean army encamped there.

6.5.1.en: The king of Israel would send watchers to the place that Elisha told him of, to verify what he told him, and to make sure of the truth of what he had foretold him ... Elisha's warnings to the king were repeated many times, and King Jehoram always took heed.

6.5.2.en: By God's guidance of Elisha and his uncovering of the plans of the king of Aram, two things were accomplished:

6.5.3.en: 1- A proof to the king of Israel that God is with him, by the tongue of His prophet Elisha, that he might believe and submit and repent of his sins, namely the worship of idols. But sadly, although the king of Israel verified the truth of Elisha's word, which protected him from every ambush the king of Aram set, he did not repent of his sins and leave the idols. It is certain that Elisha had warned him much to leave the idols.

6.5.4.en: 2- By this He declared to the king of Aram the power of God in His people Israel, that perhaps he might believe in God and leave his idols, especially after the event of the healing of the commander of his army from leprosy (ch. 5).

6.6.0.en: Which of us is for the king of Israel: who is a spy for the king of Israel.

6.6.1.en: The king of Aram was troubled by this matter, so he gathered his commanders and asked them to uncover the person among them who was plotting against him for the benefit of the king of Israel.

6.6.2.en: The king of Aram suspected treachery within his ranks, while the idea of God's intervention was always outside his thinking. So the world also thinks, ascribing the events of life to various causes, more than they see the hand of God in all of them.

6.7.0.en: One of his commanders answered him that it was not so, that there was no traitor plotting against the king for the benefit of the king of Aram, but that Elisha the prophet, who is in Israel, has all the secrets revealed to him by God and tells the king of Israel the most precise details of the plans that the king of Aram lays in the greatest secrecy, even in his bedchamber. It is strange that the king of Aram did not understand for himself the power of God that was in Elisha, despite the healing of the commander of his army, Naaman, from leprosy at Elisha's hand; but one of the servants of the king of Aram understood this truth and drew the king's attention to it. Perhaps this private servant close to the king was his army commander Naaman, with whom the miracle happened, who believed in God and in His prophet Elisha.

6.8.0.en: Dothan: a town near Shechem (Nablus). Its place today is a deserted mound called "Tell Dothan," about eighteen kilometers east of Samaria.

6.8.1.en: Because the king of Aram did not believe in God, he thought that Elisha was like one of the sorcerers, so that if he seized him and took him to his kingdom he could deprive the king of Israel of his guidance, and the king of Aram himself would use him, and he would guide him in his war plans. He did not understand that Elisha is the voice of God, who knows everything and supports only those who believe in Him, and hates evil and the worship of idols; he did not even understand that his power is nothing before the power of God that is in Elisha, and thought it easy to seize him, for he was merely a man. But he will learn, as will appear in the following verses, the irresistible power of God.

6.9.0.en: A great host (lit. heavy): that is, large, armed and trained for fighting.

6.9.1.en: The king of Aram sent a huge military force which reached Dothan by night and surrounded the city, for he felt that Elisha was a great sorcerer who needed great force, so that he might not escape them by his cunning and sorcery. Here he reminds us of the sending of many forces and soldiers to seize Christ in the garden of Gethsemane, though He was one unarmed person.

6.10.0.en: Early the next morning, when Elisha's servant rose and went out and looked around, behold, an army surrounded the city. The servant was alarmed and ran to his master to tell him how they should act in facing this great army. This shows the weakness of the servant's faith, which is completely different from the faith of his master Elisha, for he was alarmed when he heard the sound of the horses and chariots and rose early to see them, and so his fear and despair increased.

6.11.0.en: Elisha reassured his disciple, saying: "Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them," because the faith of mighty Elisha made him trust in the power of God that supports him, then he saw the heavens filled with hosts of angels, so his faith was strengthened and he reassured his disciple.

6.11.1.en: Fear not. This word is repeated often in the books of the Old and New Testaments. It is repeated constantly so that the believer besieged by difficulties and sorrows may be certain of the Lord's intervention by the working of His grace.

6.12.0.en: Elisha prayed and asked the Lord to open his servant's eyes that he might see. The Lord opened the servant's eyes, and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about them. We see here that Elisha's intercession for his disciple gave him grace to see this vision. We note that it is of the same kind as the Aramean army surrounding the city (v. 14), that is, chariots and horses, but of fire, that is, heavenly and immeasurably stronger than human soldiers and earthly chariots, so that the servant might be completely reassured; as for Elisha, he was assured even without seeing this vision, because of his strong faith.

6.13.0.en: When the army of Aram advanced toward Elisha, he prayed to the Lord, asking that the members of this army all be struck with blindness. The Lord answered Elisha's prayer and smote them with blindness. Thus we see Elisha's courage and great faith, which made him go down himself in assurance because God was with him, to meet these great armies. When the armies saw a person advancing toward them, since they were standing on a high place, they came down to him, and in the meantime Elisha prayed that God smite them with blindness, not because he was afraid of them, but that they might know that the power of God surpasses all human power, and perhaps they would understand that their pagan life far from God is error and blindness, and realize that there is a power in the people of God to which they must submit, namely the power of God, the only God above all gods.

6.14.0.en: Elisha advanced toward the blind army. The blindness here was not complete, according to the interpretation of the original Greek word, for it does not mean the complete loss of sight but the loss of the ability to distinguish, to distinguish persons and things, that is, a great weakness of sight, and this of course made all the Aramean warriors feel their weakness, so they were easily led by the word of the man who spoke to them, who was Elisha, though they did not know him. He said to them, This is not the way, neither is this the city, meaning that it was not the way God had chosen nor the city God wanted them to reach. He promised them that he would bring them to the man whom they sought, that is, Elisha, so they were reassured, and because of their weakness they submitted, and he led them on the road to Samaria, which is about eighteen kilometers from Dothan, that is, they walked several hours until they reached Samaria with Elisha.

6.14.1.en: Elisha did not want to destroy them by the power of God, or to send them back to their country in this weakness, but wanted to declare to them the power of God which they did not know, so he led them to the capital of the kingdom of Israel, which is Samaria. There, when they would find themselves surrounded by the soldiers of the children of Israel, he forgave them and fed them, so that they might feel the power of God in Elisha, who was able to destroy them but forgave them, that perhaps they would believe in his powerful and merciful God.

6.15.0.en: Elisha reached Samaria with the army of the Arameans and brought them into the great square in the city, and the armies of the children of Israel gathered to surround this strange blind army. Then Elisha prayed, and the eyes of the Aramean army were opened, and they were surprised to find themselves in the midst of Samaria, surrounded by the armies of the children of Israel, and that Elisha stood before them and that he was the one who had led them all this way from Dothan to Samaria. They were very afraid and trembled, whether at the power of the man of God who had led them on the way and now stood before them, or at the power of the armies around them. Elisha did not threaten them, but the power of God in him troubled them. He is a type here of Christ at His arrest, how the soldiers feared Him when He told them that He was the Christ, and they fell on their faces from fear (Jn 18:6). They did not know what Elisha would do with them, whether he would torture them, or kill them, or ....

6.16.0.en: When Joram king of Israel saw all that had happened in the midst of Samaria, he believed in the power of God in Elisha and felt like a little child before his father and did not know what to do. So he asked Elisha, My father, shall I smite them? Shall I smite them? That is, he would command his armies to destroy them.

6.17.0.en: Elisha forbade Joram to harm any of the Arameans. He said to him, You have not fought and taken captive these enemies that you should kill them, but this army has come in peace to our city, so they are our guests and we ought to honor them. So he offered them a feast to eat and drink, for they were tired from traveling on foot from Dothan to Samaria. These words have many effects, which are:

6.17.1.en: 1- It shows Elisha's love for his enemies; they tried to seize him and he honors them and entertains them. He carried out the commandment "Love your enemies," which Christ said hundreds of years before He said it (Mt 5:44).

6.17.2.en: 2- It is a lesson for the king of Israel and all the people of God in loving enemies, pardon and forgiveness.

6.17.3.en: 3- He gave a lesson in hospitality to strangers, even if they are enemies.

6.17.4.en: 4- A lesson the Arameans will not forget in knowing the power of the God of Israel, who is able to destroy them, for He smote them with blindness, and at the same time forgives them and even entertains them, so they feel the weakness of their gods, who did not protect them from this great God. At the same time they come to this merciful God, who entertained them and fed them, that perhaps they would finally believe in God.

6.17.5.en: 5- They would feel the uselessness of human plans and of their king's cleverness in trying to seize Elisha, for all this is nothing before the power of God.

6.18.0.en: The king of Israel carried out Elisha's command, and prepared a feast for them, and they ate and drank, then he sent them away free, and they returned to their king. Because of this the armies of Aram refrained from invading Israel for a period of time.

6.19.0.en: Samaria: it was the capital of the kingdom of Israel, which worshipped God but at the same time worshipped idols. Since God was angry with it, God allowed it the siege and the famine.

6.19.1.en: Peace with the king of Aram did not last a long time. The king of Aram forgot Israel's kindness to his army, when Elisha forgave them and fed them, so Benhadad king of Aram gathered his army and advanced toward Samaria and besieged it. This siege caused a severe famine. It is strange that Elisha feeds the Arameans, while the king of Aram besieges Samaria to put it into a severe famine. Why do we forget the kindness of others to us?!

6.20.0.en: Because of the length and harshness of the siege a famine came upon the city and prices rose to unbearable limits. An ass's head was sold for fourscore pieces of silver (four hundred and sixty grams) and the fourth part of a cab (half a liter) of dove's dung for five pieces of silver (thirty grams). From this we understand that if the ass, which is not eaten, was at this price, the animals that are eaten would be far dearer. The famine was something God had announced beforehand to His people in the Law of Moses, that when they turned away from Him, by their worship of idols, they would be exposed to famines as discipline for them (Deut 28:56, 57).

6.21.0.en: The wall: it was broad, so that a number of men walked on it, and a parapet was built on it to protect those who passed on it from the enemy's arrows.

6.21.1.en: While the king of Israel was inspecting his forces, passing along the wall of the city, a woman cried out to the king for help, saying, "Help, my lord, O king."

6.22.0.en: Barnfloor: the place where grain is gathered after harvesting, and it is called the threshing floor.

6.22.1.en: Winepress: where grapes are pressed and the juice is turned into wine, or olives are pressed to give oil.

6.22.2.en: The king answered this woman who cried out to him, that if God did not save her by lifting the siege and removing the famine, how could he save her, or from where could he bring her food? From the barnfloor empty of any grain, or from the winepress which had no grape juice?

6.23.0.en: Then the king asked her what ailed her, and she answered: A woman said, Give thy son, that we may eat him to day, and we will eat my son tomorrow. This shows the extent of the brutality to which the people had come, as a result of their worship of idols, for at hunger they lost the feelings of motherhood, which is a natural instinct, and their hands reached out to eat their children, in a cruelty beyond expression, because they had been accustomed, to please the gods, to offer their children as sacrifices to the idols.

6.24.0.en: She told the king how the two had agreed to eat their children, so they boiled the first woman's child and ate him, then when the turn of the second mother came, she hid her child. The first woman asked the king to do her justice and to command the second woman to give her her child, that they might eat him as they had agreed. It is a disturbing story, which shows the violence of the famine, which disturbs the king, or any person who hears it.

6.25.0.en: When the king heard the woman's words he rent his clothes as he was inspecting the wall, and his men around him saw that he had sackcloth upon his flesh, for the king could not bear what his people had come to in brutality as a result of the famine. The rending of clothes was a well-known Eastern custom and still exists in some countries such as Upper Egypt. The king's wearing sackcloth shows the extent of his grief and his supplication to God, but sadly he did not remove the idols, so his heart was still not upright before God, though he was grieved because of the famine. Perhaps the king's wearing sackcloth underneath was intended to hide his grief so as not to grieve his people.

6.26.0.en: God do so and more also to me: an oath meaning that he must carry out what he says or else God will bring many afflictions upon him.

6.26.1.en: The head of Elisha shall stand on him: that is, he will cut off his head.

6.26.2.en: It seems that Elisha had rebuked Jehoram king of Israel for his worship of idols and threatened him that if he did not repent of this, his land would be exposed to famine, as God commanded in (Deut 28:56, 57). Perhaps the king of Israel had asked Elisha to lift the siege and remove the famine, and Elisha did not pray for it to be lifted until God's discipline was completed and they repented of the worship of idols. The king may have been accusing Elisha of not removing the famine, as being able to do so, though the king had not asked him but sees the famine and keeps silent and does nothing.

6.26.3.en: For all this, when the king of Israel felt the harshness of the famine, to the point that mothers eat their children, he was very angry, and instead of returning in repentance to God that He might lift the distress from him, he decided that the cause of the famine was Elisha and declared that he would kill him that day. This means Jehoram's immersion in evil and condemnation, for the famine showed the hardness of his heart and his insistence on the worship of idols, and consequently his deserving of this discipline.

6.26.4.en: When distresses meet you, know that they are by God's permission, and examine yourself, for perhaps there is a sin within that is the cause of this distress; repent of it and do not throw the blame on others, or circumstances, and then you gain your soul and are delivered from every evil and receive God's mercies.

6.27.0.en: Hold the door fast: prevent him from entering, by shutting the door in his face, so that he is forced to stand before the door.

6.27.1.en: When Jehoram (Joram) declared that he would kill Elisha that day, Elisha was sitting in his house with a group of the elders of Israel around him, and God informed him of what the king intended, namely to kill him. So he said to the elders sitting around him, King Jehoram has sent a messenger to kill me now, and the king will follow this messenger; therefore Elisha asked one of his men to shut the door of the house, so that the king's messenger would not enter and kill him. He called King Jehoram the son of a murderer, because his father King Ahab had killed Naboth the Jezreelite. Elisha was not afraid of the king's messenger who was coming to kill him, but waited for the king to arrive, because Jehoram, after commanding Elisha's killing, repented and followed his messenger to prevent him from killing Elisha; and Elisha also waited for the king to arrive so as to declare the word of God before the king.

6.28.0.en: While Elisha was speaking to the elders and telling them of the king's intention to kill him by means of a messenger coming to the house and told them, Shut the door, the messenger actually reached the door and found it shut and remained standing until the king caught up with him, and the king prevented his messenger from trying to kill Elisha. Here Elisha commanded the door to be opened and went out to meet King Jehoram and his messenger, and then the king declared his rebellion against God and his despair of escape from the hands of the Arameans, and perhaps he had even decided to surrender the city to the Arameans; so the king said that this evil, that is, the famine, is of the Lord, and that he would not wait for deliverance from the Lord, because Elisha His prophet does not move to rescue the situation. Thus the king reached complete despair. Here the grace of God will intervene to announce the solution and deliverance, after man's complete helplessness, and God is longsuffering toward this wicked king and his people who still worship idols, and rescues them from death, that perhaps they would believe and repent. This is what we shall see at the beginning of the next chapter in the first two verses. And if man, like Jehoram (Joram), throws the blame on God when a trial comes upon him, God bears with him and rescues him from the trial, that perhaps he will take heed to the cause of the trial and know that it is discipline from God, that he may repent of his sins. The lifting of the siege and the end of the famine
